summary: MPLS ping and traceroute (RFC 8029) and the Segment Routing extensions (RFC 8287) help check that control plane and data plane agree. When only some transit nodes support them, testing can fail. This document defines procedures for validating the egress of a path in such partly upgraded networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine checking a mail route when only some post offices know how to answer your questions. This gives a way to still confirm the letter reaches the right final stop.

subtitle: A small extra field that lets an MPLS ping or traceroute confirm it really reached the intended end of a path.

tldr.problem: When an MPLS echo request uses only Nil FECs, no router can tell whether it is the intended egress, so a packet can be misforwarded to the wrong destination and the echo reply might still report success.
tldr.mechanism: The headend adds a new Egress TLV (type 32771) carrying the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the path's egress. The receiving router checks that address against its own interfaces and loopbacks and replies with a distinct return code.
tldr.outcome: The egress can be validated without upgrading transit nodes. Nodes that do not understand the TLV fall back to the plain Nil FEC behaviour of RFC 8029.

facts.label: Placement
facts.value: Before the Target FEC Stack TLV

today: RFC 9655 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2024, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Ping and Traceroute Need Help
sections.content:
RFC 8029 defines the MPLS echo request and echo reply, a probe and a response used to detect data plane failures in Label Switched Paths (LSPs). RFC 8287 adds Segment Routing (SR) extensions. Together they check that the data plane agrees with the control plane, and they can walk each Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) path.

That validation works through the Target FEC Stack TLV, and it assumes every node has implemented the validation procedures. In real networks only some transit nodes may have been upgraded. Controllers also build explicit paths across several domains by stacking labels, and the headend router may know nothing about the FEC behind a label. Operators still want to ping and trace these paths.

The scope is the MPLS data plane. Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A test message that checks every stop only works if every stop knows how to answer. Many stops are old and do not, but people still want to test the whole trip.

sections.title: The Problem with the Nil FEC
sections.content:
The Nil FEC is the escape route that RFC 8029 provides. It carries just a label and no other information, so a path can be traversed without validation when the FEC is unknown or routers are not upgraded. The Generic IPv4 and IPv6 prefix FECs add some validation, but the RFC says they are not thoroughly detailed in RFC 8029 and may not be widely supported.

This document uses a single Nil FEC to stand for the whole label stack, however many segments it has. RFC 8029 says that if the outermost FEC is the Nil FEC, a node MUST skip the Target FEC validation completely. As a result, a router cannot decide whether it is the intended egress. The packet may be misforwarded to an incorrect destination while the echo reply still returns success.

A successful reply does not prove the probe reached the right place when every label is a Nil FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: If every label is just a blank sticker, nobody can tell if the parcel went to the right house. It might land at the wrong door and the test would still say it worked.

sections.title: The Egress TLV
sections.content:
The fix is a new optional Egress TLV. It MAY be included in an MPLS echo request. If present it MUST appear before the Target FEC Stack TLV, and it can only be used in requests generated by the headend node of the LSP or SR Policy being verified.

The TLV has three fields. Type is 32771. Length is 4 octets for an IPv4 address or 16 octets for an IPv6 address, and it excludes the Type and Length fields themselves. Address carries the valid IPv4 or IPv6 address of the egress of the path, corresponding to the last label in the stack or to the SR Policy Endpoint field.

When several Nil FECs are present, the Egress TLV must correspond to the ultimate egress of the label stack. Explicit paths can be built from Node-SID, Adj-SID, Binding SID and so on, but the address always comes from the path's egress or destination.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note has a label, a size, and the address of the last stop. The sender writes it and puts it in front of everything else.

sections.title: How the Headend Builds the Request
sections.content:
In ping mode, when the Target FEC Stack holds a single Nil FEC for the last segment of the SR Policy path, the sender MUST add an Egress TLV with the address from the SR Policy Endpoint field. The label value in the Nil FEC MAY be zero when one Nil FEC stands for many labels. If the endpoint is not specified or is zero, the sender MUST use the address of the last segment of the policy.

  • If the last SID is an Adj-SID, the address comes from the node at the remote end of that adjacency.
  • If the last SID is a Binding SID, the address comes from the last node of the path the Binding SID represents.

Traceroute mode follows the same rule. An implementation MAY send multiple Nil FECs if that is easier. If it does, the last one MUST correspond to the Egress TLV, and its label MAY be zero. A zero or missing endpoint again means using the address of the last segment endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender looks at the last stop on the route and writes that stop's address in the note. If the route does not say where it ends, the sender works it out from the final step.

sections.title: How Receivers Check the Address
sections.content:
This document does not change how a node processes the Nil FEC itself. The Egress TLV does not affect validation of a Target FEC Stack sub-TLV that is not a Nil FEC. Extra processing MUST be done on the receiver, where RSC is the Return Subcode:

  1. If Label-stack-depth is greater than 0 and the sub-TLV at FEC-stack-depth is a Nil FEC, set Best-return-code to 8 and Best-rtn-subcode to Label-stack-depth, which reports transit switching.
  2. If Label-stack-depth is 0 and the sub-TLV is a Nil FEC, look for an exact match of the Egress TLV address among the locally configured interface and loopback addresses. A match sets Best-return-code to 36. No match sets it to 10.
  3. If the headend sent multiple Nil FECs, then once the stack is used up or a label with the Bottom-of-Stack bit set to 1 is processed, all Nil FEC sub-TLVs MUST be removed and the Egress TLV MUST be validated.

In ping mode the destination is the only receiver. In traceroute every node is a receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Stops in the middle just say that they passed the parcel along. The last stop checks the address on the note against its own addresses and says yes, this is me, or no, it is not.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The extension is backward compatible with RFC 8029. A router that does not support the Egress TLV ignores it and uses the Nil FEC procedures. RFC 8029 and RFC 9041 allow such a node to silently drop the TLV, step over it, or send an error message.

  • If the egress does not support it, egress validation is not done and the reply carries Best-return-code 3, meaning the replying router is an egress for the FEC at the stack depth.
  • If a transit node does not support it, the reply carries Best-return-code 8 with the Label-stack-depth, reporting transit switching.
  • If a transit node drops or steps over the TLV, the headend keeps sending it, so a supporting egress can still validate. If a transit node answers with an error, the headend logs it and continues with the TTL incremented.
sections.plainLanguage: Old post offices that do not understand the note simply ignore it and carry on. The test still runs, it just cannot confirm the final address.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added two entries to the registry group for MPLS LSP Ping Parameters. In the TLVs registry, type 32771 is named Egress TLV with reference RFC 9655. In the Return Codes registry, value 36 means the replying router is an egress for the address in the Egress TLV for the FEC at stack depth <RSC>.
sections.plainLanguage: The number 32771 and the answer code 36 were written into the official list, so everyone uses the same numbers for the same things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines one additional TLV for MPLS LSP ping and conforms to the mechanisms of RFC 8029. All the security considerations of RFC 8287 apply. The RFC states that it does not introduce any additional security challenges.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note follows the same safety rules as the old messages, so it adds no new danger.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 4 octets for IPv4 or 16 for IPv6; excludes Type and Length.

fields.name: Address
fields.desc: Address of the path egress (4 or 16 octets).

viz.caption: RETURN CODES USED BY THE EGRESS CHECK

items.label: Egress (no validation)
items.desc: Replying router is an egress for the FEC at stack-depth; sent when the egress does not support the TLV.

items.label: Label switched
items.desc: Label switched at stack-depth; reports transit switching.

items.label: Address mismatch
items.desc: Mapping for this FEC is not the given label at stack-depth; Egress TLV address lookup failed.

items.label: Egress for address
items.desc: Replying router is an egress for the address in the Egress TLV.
